newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed after volatile session.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed after volatile session.

text.p: The dollar fell against the German mark Wednesday as German officials hinted they will not lower interest rates soon, but rallied against the Japanese yen on an unconfirmed report that Washington approves of the dollar's recent rally.
Otmar Issing, chief economist at Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, said in a German television interview that he saw no reason to expect lower interest rates.
Steady or higher interest rates tend to boost a nation's currency by raising the relative value of domestic investments.
The mark surged on Issing's comment, reaching its highest level in three and a half years against the yen, and also gained on the dollar.
"We continue to see tremendous demand for marks, especially against the yen. It's coming from every sector of the world," said John Hazelton, chief currency dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.

The dollar also slumped against the yen in early trading, but later rebounded. A report from financial news agency Bridge News appeared to fuel dollar buying. It quoted an unidentified source claiming the Clinton administration will not attempt to weaken the dollar in order to reduce the persistent U.S. trade gap with Japan.
As the dollar rises against the yen, U.S. exports to Japan become more expensive, while Japanese import prices fall.
Administration officials have consistently stated in public that they want a strong dollar.
But another anonymous news report Tuesday claimed the administration feared the rising dollar would worsen the trade picture. Wednesday's report seemed to refute that story.
"It was a contradiction of the statement (Tuesday), and it gave the dollar room to go back up again," said Vincent Amaru, a foreign exchange vice president at Citibank.
The dollar fell to 1.5212 marks from 1.5254 late Tuesday. It rebounded from early lows against the yen to break 113 yen for the first time in 33 months, ending at 112.93 yen, up from 112.29 Tuesday.
The dollar ended slightly lower at 1.2532 Swiss francs, from 1.2540 Tuesday. The British pound fell to $1.5979 from $1.5991. The dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3437 from C$1.3454.
The yen also suffered from comments by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita that suggested Japanese interest rates will stay low for the foreseeable future.
Matsushita told a meeting of Bank of Japan deputies that the Japanese economy would likely grow slowly and that market expectations for higher Japanese interest rates had abated.
"It's not so much dollar strength as it is yen weakness that we're seeing," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank New York.
Late in New York trading, the mark got a modest boost from the Bank of Italy, which announced a surprising cut in its key discount rate to 7.5 percent from 8.25 percent.
The mark climbed against the Italian lira and also rose against the dollar.
"The mark remains strong against everything. The dollar is just holding its own," said Amaru.
